details:
**Koans**
Paradoxical questions, statements, or anecdotes that Zen students contemplate in order to break through ordinary logical thought and reach enlightenment. Famous examples include "What is the sound of one hand clapping?" and "If you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him."

**Bodhidharma**
The legendary monk, said to come from South India or Persia/Central Asia, who brought Zen (Chan) to China and is revered as its first patriarch. He supposedly spent nine years gazing at a cave wall and cut off his eyelids after falling asleep; nicknamed the "Blue-Eyed Barbarian," he is depicted in Japanese Daruma dolls and credited with exercises that grew into Shaolin martial arts.

**Flower Sermon**
The wordless sermon from which Zen claims its origin, in which the Buddha silently held up a white flower (often a lotus) and only his disciple Mahakashyapa understood and smiled. It is considered the first "mind-to-mind" transmission of enlightenment outside the scriptures.

**The Blue Cliff Record**
A Song-dynasty Chinese collection of 100 koans with verse and prose commentary, compiled in the 12th century. It is especially important in the Rinzai school.

**The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan)**
A 13th-century Song-dynasty collection of 48 koans compiled by the monk Wumen Huikai. Its first case, in which Zhaozhou answers "Wu" (Japanese "Mu," meaning "no" or "nothing") when asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, is one of the most famous koans.

**Rinzai and Soto**
The two main schools of Japanese Zen. Rinzai, descended from the Chinese master Linji, emphasizes koan practice to provoke sudden enlightenment, while Soto emphasizes quiet sitting meditation; a smaller third Japanese school is Obaku.

**Satori and kensho**
Japanese terms for enlightenment experiences in Zen. Kensho means "seeing one's true nature," an initial insight, while satori refers more broadly to sudden awakening or understanding.

**Dogen and shikantaza**
Dogen was the 13th-century Japanese monk who founded the Soto school after studying in China. He taught shikantaza ("just sitting"), a form of zazen meditation without any object of focus such as a koan.

**Huike**
Dazu Huike, the second patriarch of Chan after Bodhidharma. According to legend, Bodhidharma agreed to teach him only after Huike cut off his own left arm to prove his sincerity.

**Zen gardens**
Japanese dry landscape (karesansui) gardens of carefully placed rocks and raked gravel or sand, designed as aids to contemplation. The rock garden at Ryoan-ji in Kyoto is the most famous example.

**Huineng and the mirror verse**
Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, won the patriarchate with a verse answering a rival's poem about polishing the mind like a mirror: since the bright mirror has no stand and fundamentally nothing exists, there is nowhere for dust to land. The episode is recounted in the Platform Sutra and is associated with the doctrine of sudden enlightenment.

**Sesshin and oryoki**
Sesshin is an intensive, highly regimented Zen meditation retreat, during which practitioners may experience illusory visions called makyo. Oryoki is the formal ritual style of eating from nested bowls practiced during such retreats.

**Chan, Seon, and Thien**
The names of Zen in China, Korea, and Vietnam, respectively; all derive from the Sanskrit "dhyana," meaning meditation. "Zen" is the Japanese pronunciation of the same word.

**Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp**
An 11th-century Chinese chronicle of the lineage of Chan patriarchs and masters. It reflects the Zen concept of "transmission," the unbroken passing of enlightened understanding from teacher to student.

**Five Ranks**
A poem by the Chinese master Dongshan Liangjie, founder of the Caodong school (the Chinese ancestor of Soto), describing five stages in realizing the relationship between the absolute and the relative.
